```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

You and Simonsson (2026) predicted 2-month sputum culture conversion in the
REMoxTB tuberculosis trial with machine-learning classifiers. The features
for those classifiers came from two nonlinear mixed-effects early
bactericidal activity (EBA) models of the MGIT liquid-culture time to
positivity (TTP), fitted in NONMEM to the first 14 and the first 28 days of
treatment. The classifiers themselves are not models nlmixr2lib can carry;
the two TTP models are:

* `You_2026_moxifloxacin_ttp14d` -- biexponential model for days 0-14
  (Methods Equation 2, Supplementary Table S2).
* `You_2026_moxifloxacin_ttp28d` -- exponential approach to an asymptote
  for days 0-28 (Methods Equation 3, Supplementary Table S3).

Neither model has a drug-exposure term. TTP is a function of time on
treatment, the treatment arm and baseline covariates only, so the models
have no dosing events and no differential equations. Time is in days and
TTP in hours.

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("You_2026_moxifloxacin_ttp14d"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1111/cts.70694>

REMoxTB (NCT00864383) randomised adults with drug-sensitive pulmonary
tuberculosis to a control regimen of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide
and ethambutol (HRZE) or to one of two 4-month regimens in which
moxifloxacin replaced ethambutol (the "isoniazid group", HRZM) or
isoniazid (the "ethambutol group", MRZE). The covariate columns
`TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ETHAMBUTOL` and `TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ISONIAZID`
name the arms after the drug moxifloxacin replaced; the paper's tables
name them after the companion drug that was kept.

# Population

You 2026 prints no demographics table. The analysis dataset held 1821
patients (Results, "Clinical Data"). The baseline characteristics below
are from Table 1 of the primary REMoxTB report (Gillespie 2014, N Engl J
Med 371:1577-1587, per-protocol population, N = 1548): 70% male; 44%
Black, 31% Asian, 25% mixed race, <1% other; 31% current smokers; 71% with
lung cavitation; 7% HIV-positive; age 30% < 25 y, 31% 25-35 y, 39% > 35 y;
weight 10% < 40 kg, 16% 40-45 kg, 40% > 45-55 kg, 32% > 55-75 kg, 2% >
75 kg; baseline MGIT TTP >= 5 days in 51%. Patients were randomised in
South Africa, India, Tanzania, Kenya, Thailand, Malaysia, Zambia, China
and Mexico.

# The printed equations have sign errors

As printed, Equation 2 is `TTP = e^Abi * e^(-alpha t) + e^Bbi * e^(-beta t)`
and Equation 3 is `TTP = Aexp + Bexp * (1 - e^(alpha t))`. With the
positive slopes of Tables S2 and S3 both would make TTP fall with time on
treatment, and Equation 3 would go negative within days. Figure 3 and the
reported medians (TTP rising by 182 h over 14 days and by 240 h over 28
days) show TTP rising, which is what effective treatment does: fewer viable
bacteria take longer to turn a culture positive. The models therefore use
`exp(+alpha t)`, `exp(+beta t)` and `1 - exp(-alpha t)`. The check below
shows that the corrected typical curves start at the reported median
baseline and rise by about the reported amounts; the printed signs fail it.

```{r typical}
mod14 <- readModelDb("You_2026_moxifloxacin_ttp14d")
mod28 <- readModelDb("You_2026_moxifloxacin_ttp28d")

# Reference covariates: cavitation present, male, non-smoker, Black or mixed
# race, at the age, weight and baseline-TTP centres.
ref_cov <- data.frame(
  LUNG_CAVITY = 1, SEXF = 0, SMOKE = 0, RACE_ASIAN = 0, RACE_BLACK = 0,
  RACE_MISSING = 0, AGE = 31.3, WT = 51.0, TTP_MGIT_BASE = 126.8 / 24
)
arms <- data.frame(
  arm = c("Control (HRZE)", "Isoniazid group (HRZM)", "Ethambutol group (MRZE)"),
  TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ETHAMBUTOL = c(0, 1, 0),
  TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ISONIAZID = c(0, 0, 1)
)
typ_events <- function(days) {
  merge(arms, ref_cov) |>
    dplyr::mutate(id = seq_len(dplyr::n())) |>
    merge(data.frame(time = days)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(evid = 0L, amt = 0) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time)
}
typ14 <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod14), typ_events(c(0, 14)),
  keep = "arm", returnType = "data.frame"
)
typ28 <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod28), typ_events(c(0, 28)),
  keep = "arm", returnType = "data.frame"
)

closed14 <- function(t, alpha, b, beta) exp(3.43) * exp(alpha * t) + exp(b) * exp(beta * t)
closed28 <- function(t, alpha, b) 117 + b * (1 - exp(-alpha * t))
closed <- data.frame(
  arm = arms$arm,
  alpha14 = c(0.0419, 0.0477, 0.0477), b14 = c(4.54, 4.56, 4.56), beta14 = c(0.0645, 0.0737, 0.0737),
  alpha28 = c(0.0472, 0.0441, 0.0599), b28 = c(341, 425, 341)
)
chk_typ <- closed |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    base14_closed = closed14(0, alpha14, b14, beta14),
    day14_closed = closed14(14, alpha14, b14, beta14),
    base28_closed = closed28(0, alpha28, b28),
    day28_closed = closed28(28, alpha28, b28),
    day14_printed_signs = exp(3.43) * exp(-alpha14 * 14) + exp(b14) * exp(-beta14 * 14),
    day28_printed_signs = 117 + b28 * (1 - exp(alpha28 * 28))
  )
model_typ <- data.frame(
  arm = arms$arm,
  base14_model = typ14$ttp[typ14$time == 0],
  day14_model = typ14$ttp[typ14$time == 14],
  base28_model = typ28$ttp[typ28$time == 0],
  day28_model = typ28$ttp[typ28$time == 28]
)
chk_typ <- dplyr::left_join(chk_typ, model_typ, by = "arm")

chk_typ |>
  dplyr::select(arm, base14_model, day14_model, day14_printed_signs, base28_model, day28_model, day28_printed_signs) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Arm" = arm, "Day 0, 14-d model" = base14_model, "Day 14, 14-d model" = day14_model,
    "Day 14, printed signs" = day14_printed_signs, "Day 0, 28-d model" = base28_model,
    "Day 28, 28-d model" = day28_model, "Day 28, printed signs" = day28_printed_signs
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Typical TTP (h) for the reference subject, corrected vs printed exponent signs.")

stopifnot(
  # The solved model is the closed form (same parameters, no randomness).
  max(abs(chk_typ$base14_model - chk_typ$base14_closed)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(chk_typ$day14_model - chk_typ$day14_closed)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(chk_typ$base28_model - chk_typ$base28_closed)) < 1e-6,
  max(abs(chk_typ$day28_model - chk_typ$day28_closed)) < 1e-6,
  # Corrected signs: TTP rises; printed signs: it falls (or turns negative).
  all(chk_typ$day14_model > chk_typ$base14_model),
  all(chk_typ$day14_printed_signs < chk_typ$base14_closed),
  all(chk_typ$day28_printed_signs < 0)
)
```

The reference subject's 14-day baseline, `exp(3.43) + exp(4.54)` = 124.6 h
(control) or 126.5 h (moxifloxacin arms), is within 2% of the reported
median predicted baseline of 126.8 h.

# Virtual cohort

200 subjects per arm, with covariates drawn independently from the
REMoxTB per-protocol baseline table. Within each age and weight band the
value is drawn uniformly; the open-ended bands are closed at 18-60 years
and 35-90 kg. Baseline MGIT TTP is drawn log-normally with a median of
5 days (51% of patients had a baseline TTP of at least 5 days) and a
log-scale SD of 0.45; the paper gives no distribution for it.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(2026)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2026)
n_arm <- 200L
draw_band <- function(n, breaks, probs) {
  band <- sample(seq_along(probs), n, replace = TRUE, prob = probs)
  stats::runif(n, breaks[band], breaks[band + 1])
}
race <- sample(c("Black", "Asian", "Mixed", "Missing"), 3 * n_arm,
  replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.44, 0.31, 0.24, 0.01)
)
cohort <- data.frame(
  id = seq_len(3 * n_arm),
  arm = rep(arms$arm, each = n_arm),
  TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ETHAMBUTOL = rep(arms$TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ETHAMBUTOL, each = n_arm),
  TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ISONIAZID = rep(arms$TRT_MOXIFLOXACIN_FOR_ISONIAZID, each = n_arm),
  SEXF = stats::rbinom(3 * n_arm, 1, 0.30),
  SMOKE = stats::rbinom(3 * n_arm, 1, 0.31),
  LUNG_CAVITY = stats::rbinom(3 * n_arm, 1, 0.71),
  RACE_BLACK = as.integer(race == "Black"),
  RACE_ASIAN = as.integer(race == "Asian"),
  RACE_MISSING = as.integer(race == "Missing"),
  AGE = draw_band(3 * n_arm, c(18, 25, 35, 60), c(0.30, 0.31, 0.39)),
  WT = draw_band(3 * n_arm, c(35, 40, 45, 55, 75, 90), c(0.10, 0.16, 0.40, 0.32, 0.02)),
  TTP_MGIT_BASE = stats::rlnorm(3 * n_arm, log(5), 0.45)
)
cohort |>
  dplyr::group_by(arm) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(), female = mean(SEXF), smoker = mean(SMOKE), cavity = mean(LUNG_CAVITY),
    median_age = median(AGE), median_wt = median(WT), median_ttp_base_d = median(TTP_MGIT_BASE)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Virtual cohort summary by arm.")
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
obs_events <- function(days) {
  merge(cohort, data.frame(time = days)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(evid = 0L, amt = 0) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time)
}
sim14 <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod14, obs_events(0:14), keep = "arm", returnType = "data.frame")
sim28 <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod28, obs_events(0:28), keep = "arm", returnType = "data.frame")
```

## Visual predictive check (Figure 3)

Figure 3 shows prediction-corrected VPCs per arm on a log TTP axis. The
simulated median and 2.5th/97.5th percentiles of TTP with residual error
(`sim`) are plotted on the same axes. MGIT cultures are read for at most
42 days (1008 h), so values above that are capped for display.

```{r vpc, fig.height = 6}
vpc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  sim14 |> dplyr::mutate(model = "(a) 14-day biexponential"),
  sim28 |> dplyr::mutate(model = "(b) 28-day exponential")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sim_cap = pmin(sim, 1008)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(model, arm, time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p025 = quantile(sim_cap, 0.025), p50 = median(sim_cap), p975 = quantile(sim_cap, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ggplot(vpc, aes(time, p50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = p025, ymax = p975), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p025), linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p975), linetype = 2) +
  scale_y_log10(limits = c(40, 1100)) +
  facet_grid(model ~ arm, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    x = "Time since start of treatment (days)", y = "TTP (h)",
    caption = "Replicates the layout of Figure 3 of You 2026 (median, 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles)."
  )
```

Figure 3 (a low-resolution image, read by eye) shows the median rising
from about 130 h at day 0 to about 250-300 h at day 14 and to about
350-400 h at day 28, with the 97.5th percentile near the 1000 h culture
limit after the first week. The simulation follows the same course; its
day-14 median runs somewhat higher, because the simulated individuals
carry the full between-subject variability of the right-skewed first term
(see 'Reported medians'), whereas Figure 3 is prediction-corrected. At
day 0 the simulated 2.5th-97.5th percentile interval of the 14-day model,
`r v0 <- vpc[vpc$time == 0 & grepl("14-day", vpc$model), ]; round(median(v0$p025))`-`r round(median(v0$p975))` h
(median over arms), is close to the roughly 60-400 h of Figure 3a. That spread comes mostly from
the eta on `A_bi`: with the eta read as additive on `A_bi` instead (a 21%
CV on the first-term amplitude) the upper limit would fall to about 220 h.

## Reported medians

Results reports the median predicted baseline TTP (126.8 h in both models),
the median predicted rise from day 0 to day 14 (182 h, 14-day model) and
from day 0 to day 28 (240.3 h, 28-day model). These are medians of the
individual predictions, so the comparison uses `ttp` (no residual error).

The paper's individual predictions come from empirical Bayes estimates,
which are shrunk towards the typical value (Results: 27% on the baseline
and 47% on the slope of the 14-day model; 18%, 44% and 31% on the
intercept, slope and asymptote of the 28-day model). A simulation from the
full omegas spreads the individuals more widely. In the 14-day model this
matters: `A_bi` is a log amplitude with an exponential eta, so the first
term `exp(A_bi)` is strongly right-skewed and its spread lifts the median
rise. The cohort is therefore also simulated with each omega scaled by
`(1 - shrinkage)^2`, which approximates the spread of the empirical Bayes
estimates.

```{r medians}
diag_omega <- function(v) {
  m <- diag(v, length(v))
  dimnames(m) <- list(names(v), names(v))
  m
}
omega14_ebe <- diag_omega(c(etaa_bi = 0.0427 * (1 - 0.27)^2, etalslope_bi = 0.785 * (1 - 0.47)^2))
omega28_ebe <- diag_omega(c(
  etala_exp = 0.0788 * (1 - 0.18)^2, etalalpha_exp = 0.34 * (1 - 0.44)^2,
  etalb_exp = 0.227 * (1 - 0.31)^2
))
sim14_ebe <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod14, obs_events(c(0, 14)), omega = omega14_ebe, returnType = "data.frame")
sim28_ebe <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod28, obs_events(c(0, 28)), omega = omega28_ebe, returnType = "data.frame")

median_rise <- function(sim, day_end) {
  d0 <- sim |> dplyr::filter(time == 0) |> dplyr::arrange(id)
  d1 <- sim |> dplyr::filter(time == day_end) |> dplyr::arrange(id)
  c(base = median(d0$ttp), rise = median(d1$ttp - d0$ttp))
}
m14 <- median_rise(sim14, 14)
m14_ebe <- median_rise(sim14_ebe, 14)
m28 <- median_rise(sim28, 28)
m28_ebe <- median_rise(sim28_ebe, 28)
chk_med <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "Median baseline TTP, 14-day model (h)", "Median baseline TTP, 28-day model (h)",
    "Median dTTP 0-14 days (h)", "Median dTTP 0-28 days (h)"
  ),
  reported = c(126.8, 126.8, 182, 240.3),
  full = c(m14[["base"]], m28[["base"]], m14[["rise"]], m28[["rise"]]),
  ebe = c(m14_ebe[["base"]], m28_ebe[["base"]], m14_ebe[["rise"]], m28_ebe[["rise"]])
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    pct_full = 100 * (full - reported) / reported,
    pct_ebe = 100 * (ebe - reported) / reported
  )
chk_med |>
  dplyr::select(quantity, reported, full, pct_full, ebe, pct_ebe) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Quantity" = quantity, "You 2026 Results" = reported,
    "Simulated, full omega" = full, "Difference (%)" = pct_full,
    "Simulated, shrunk omega" = ebe, "Difference, shrunk (%)" = pct_ebe
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Reported vs simulated medians of the individual predictions (600 subjects).")
```

The baselines and, with the shrunk omegas, the 14-day rise agree with the
paper within a few percent. The 28-day rise is above the reported 240.3 h
whichever omegas are used (by `r round(chk_med$pct_full[4])`% and
`r round(chk_med$pct_ebe[4])`% here). Even with no between-subject variability
the reference subject rises by 250 h (control), 301 h (isoniazid group) and
277 h (ethambutol group), so the median over a cohort balanced across the
arms sits near 275 h unless the covariates pull it down; with the
covariate distribution assumed here they do not. The analysis-dataset
covariate distribution and the covariate centres are not reported (see
'Assumptions and deviations'), and the parameters were not adjusted to
close the gap.

```{r medians-assert, include = FALSE}
# A mis-transcribed intercept, slope or exponent sign moves these medians
# by tens of percent. The 28-day rise carries the unexplained ~15% offset
# discussed above, so its bound is wider.
stopifnot(
  abs(chk_med$pct_ebe[1]) < 10,
  abs(chk_med$pct_ebe[2]) < 10,
  abs(chk_med$pct_ebe[3]) < 10,
  abs(chk_med$pct_ebe[4]) < 30
)
```

## NCA

There is no drug concentration in either model (the outcome is a
bacterial-load biomarker driven by time on treatment), so a PKNCA
non-compartmental analysis does not apply; the closed-form and reported-
median checks above take its place.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Exponent signs.** Equations 2 and 3 are implemented with the signs
  that make TTP rise, as shown above; the printed signs contradict
  Figure 3 and the reported medians.
* **Shared slope variability (14-day model).** Table S2 reports a single
  `omega2 slope` (0.785) with a single shrinkage value (47%) for a model
  with two slopes. It is encoded as one eta shared by `alpha_bi` and
  `beta_bi`; `B_bi` has no IIV, and the `omega2 baseline` eta acts
  exponentially on `A_bi` itself (which is a log amplitude).
* **Covariate functional form.** No covariate equation is printed. The
  stepwise covariate model was run in PsN, whose default linear form is
  `P * (1 + theta)` for a binary covariate and `P * (1 + theta * (x -
  median))` for a continuous one; that form is used, applied to `A_bi` and
  `B_bi` on their log scale. It is supported by the agreement between the
  two models: the absence of cavitation raises the typical baseline by 13%
  in the 14-day model (via `A_bi`) and by 15% in the 28-day model (via
  `A_exp`), and smoking by 5.7% and 5.6%. Reading the 14-day effects as
  additive on `A_bi` (a factor `exp(theta)` on its term) would give 3.2%
  and 1.5% and break that agreement.
* **Covariate coding.** From the supplementary analysis code: smoking is
  the TB-PACTS substance-use occurrence flag (Y/N), read here as current
  smoking (`SMOKE`); "unknown race" pools the TB-PACTS values "NOT
  REPORTED" and "OTHER" (`RACE_MISSING`); each race effect is a separate
  indicator, so all race indicators 0 means Black or mixed race in the
  14-day model and mixed or unreported race in the 28-day model. The
  reported "absence of cavity" effects enter as `(1 - LUNG_CAVITY)`.
* **Centring values.** PsN centres continuous covariates on the
  analysis-dataset median, which You 2026 does not report. Age (31.3 y)
  and weight (51.0 kg) are the medians interpolated from the grouped age
  and weight distribution of the REMoxTB per-protocol population
  (Gillespie 2014 Table 1, which prints no medians); the You 2026 analysis
  dataset is larger (1821 patients). Baseline TTP is centred at 126.8 h,
  the median predicted baseline TTP, and is assumed to enter in hours. A
  different centre changes only subjects away from it, not the typical
  curves.
* **Arm effects.** The text says no statistically significant difference
  between the three treatments was found, yet Tables S2 and S3 list
  arm-specific slopes, intercepts and asymptotes as final estimates. The
  tables are encoded as printed. In the 14-day model the two moxifloxacin
  arms share one set of values ("isoniazid or ethambutol").
* **Virtual cohort.** Covariates are drawn independently; their
  correlations in REMoxTB are not reported. The baseline-TTP covariate is
  drawn independently of each subject's model-predicted baseline.
* **Reported 28-day rise.** The simulated median rise over 28 days is
  about 10-15% above the reported 240.3 h (see 'Reported medians'); no
  reading of the printed model closes the gap, and it is left as found.
* **Culture limits.** Neither model includes the 42-day (1008 h) upper
  limit of MGIT culture or culture-negative samples; the paper does not
  describe how they were handled in the EBA models.
